meta.title: Autonomous vehicles in Texas, 14 days of posts
meta.subject: autonomous vehicles and robotaxis in Texas — Waymo and Tesla robotaxi operations in Austin, Houston, Dallas and San Antonio, incidents and safety stories, city council and legislative reactions, state permitting at the DMV, and liability and insurance rules
meta.subtitle: Oct 19 to Nov 1, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about autonomous vehicles and robotaxis in Texas, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated weekly.

lanes.label: Cybercab scaling proves Tesla winning
lanes.description: Tesla's fast Cybercab ramp in Austin (300+ cars, 8x in a month, Dallas next) is shown as proof that Tesla's robotaxi is scaling faster than anyone and is the future of transport.

lanes.label: Tesla overtakes Waymo in Austin
lanes.description: Head-to-head claims that Waymo is losing ground, shut down, or outnumbered in Austin, and that Tesla's vertical integration and Texas factory give it the edge.

lanes.label: Cameras vs lidar in storms
lanes.description: Austin's rainstorms and night operations are used as a test of sensor strategy: Tesla's camera-only system kept running while Waymo's lidar fleet paused, versus arguments that lidar is needed for edge cases like dark roads.

lanes.label: Safety incidents and who answers
lanes.description: Safety stories and incident reports (NHTSA crashes, stuck or misrouted robotaxis, Waymo blunders, Cybercab crash photos) raise questions of accountability, remote assistance and whether rollouts are careful enough.

lanes.label: Texas as the AV proving ground
lanes.description: Texas is framed as the place where autonomy, manufacturing and the economy get built, with the Texas DMV registration and light regulation letting robotaxis expand across the Texas Triangle.

lanes.label: Rider experience, pricing and waits
lanes.description: First-hand ride reports and price and wait-time comparisons between Cybercab, Model Y robotaxi, Waymo and Uber, treated as evidence of whether robotaxis are really replacing human-driven rides.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Yoda
posts.text:
NHTSA refreshed its self-driving crash data on Oct 15, and Tesla's robotaxi fleet logged 9 reports in August, its highest month so far. The reports themselves give the fuller picture. None of the 9 involved an injury, the highest contact speed was 5 mph, and 8 of the 9 had no passenger aboard. The one trip with riders was a Model Y that was rear-ended by an SUV while stopped at a yield sign. Two reports were low-hanging chains across parking-lot entrances, two were alley contacts below half a mile per hour, and the first Cybercab report was a 5 mph parking-lot pothole with a safety monitor aboard. By city, Dallas had 5, Austin 3 and Tampa 1, Tampa being the first Florida report, while Miami and Orlando have had none since unsupervised service began there in July. Most of these happened while empty cars were moving between rides in tight spaces, not during passenger trips.

posts.name: I45_Autonomy
posts.text:
🚛 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗨𝗧𝗢𝗡𝗢𝗠𝗢𝗨𝗦 𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗖𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗥𝗘𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗜𝗦 𝗔𝗖𝗖𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 — 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗢𝗠𝗜𝗖𝗦 𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗗 𝗧𝗢 𝗜𝗚𝗡𝗢𝗥𝗘.

The Wall Street Journal's latest feature takes readers onto Texas highways, where 𝗔𝘂𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 ($AUR) is demonstrating the future of freight transportation.

🛡️ 𝗦𝗔𝗙𝗘𝗧𝗬: 𝗔𝗡 𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗚𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗟𝗬 𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗗

From July 2021 through August 2026, NHTSA recorded 69 reported fatal crashes involving automated-driving or driver-assistance systems. 𝗡𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝗸 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱-𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺. Limited deployment means this isn't yet proof of superior safety.

Aurora's long-range LiDAR and advanced perception system detect hazards early, anticipate merging vehicles, and navigate highway traffic without aggressive braking.

📊 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗢𝗠𝗜𝗖 𝗢𝗣𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗨𝗡𝗜𝗧𝗬

• $2.34/mile — average trucking operating cost
• 44% — driver wages and benefits
• 21% — fuel costs
• 10% — potential reduction in fuel consumption
• 40% — conventional truck utilization at Detmar
• 20 hours/day — Aurora's autonomous operations at Detmar

🚀 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗖𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗗𝗘𝗣𝗟𝗢𝗬𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧

• 𝗔𝘂𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗮: ~30 trucks, targeting 200 by year-end 2026
• 𝗠𝗰𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗲: Up to 10 Aurora trucks planned
• 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗺𝗮𝗿: Two Aurora trucks operating, ~30 more expected
• 𝗩𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗼: 300 autonomous trucks planned with Aurora and Waabi by the end of 2027
• 𝗜𝗞𝗘𝗔/𝗞𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗸: Preparing a 219-mile driverless Texas route

The real breakthrough isn't simply removing the driver.

𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗱𝗹𝗲.

A truck operating 20 hours a day changes fleet utilization, freight capacity, and potentially the economics of long-haul transportation.

The next major unlock could come from 𝗜𝗡𝗦𝗨𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗨𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗥𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗦. As safety data accumulates and insurers gain confidence in pricing autonomous risk, adoption barriers could fall.

𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 → 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 → 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 → 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲.

posts.name: Robotaxi Radar
posts.text:
Austin Saturday Morning Robotaxi vs. Uber Update - Insane surge pricing for Texas vs. Florida game:

🚕 Cybercab - $29.13 - 17 min wait ⏱️
🚕 Model Y - $26.11 - 28 min wait ⏱️
🚙 UberX - $24.96 - 8 min wait ⏱️
🚙 Comfort Electric - $29.98 - 7 min wait ⏱️

🔴 Every single tier on this screen set an all-time record for this route. Comfort Electric is the wildest at $29.98 against an old high of $12.99, and it's the priciest ride on the board. Tesla isn't even the most expensive EV today
 🔴 10am last Saturday for the same route: Cybercab $10.73, Model Y $9.31, UberX $6.94. That's 2.7x to 3.6x in one week
 🔴 This beats ACL. The priciest ride I logged at the Zilker gates on ACL Saturday was $22.74, and that was for a longer ride
 🧐 Uber surged and controlled its waits. UberX went 6 min to 8 min. Tesla surged AND the wait went 4 to 17 and 10 to 28

These one mile fares are off the charts. The surge brings in more Uber drivers, but it can't deploy more Tesla cars that aren’t currently registered. Lower prices will require more Robotaxi supply 🚕🚕🚕 ✍️

posts.name: Joe Hansen
posts.text:
What caught my eye in the Elon Universe on 17 Oct.

1. Robotaxi riders in Austin got an alert: rides now run 6am to midnight. The Texas registry is at 803, with 454 Model Y and 349 Cybercab. Late rides matter most for bar staff, nurses off a late shift and anyone leaving a concert.

2. Elon: "Neuralink will help millions of people," quoting Jake Schneider, who has ALS: "Neuralink has given me some of the independence back that ALS has stolen from me." Participants have used their implants for over 50,000 hours. Hearing it from a patient says more than any demo.

3. SpaceX reports Q3 on Tue 20 Oct, Tesla on Wed 21 Oct. Merger talk is all over the betting markets. Two big calls in two days. The merger stays talk until there's a filing.

4. Elon says the Roadster will do the reveal stunts by itself, and Tesla will build "a wild looping track (crazier even than Hot Wheels)" at its Texas HQ. Stunts like that belong on a closed track, and Texas HQ will have one.

5. Starlink posted a statement on India, and Elon replied "Much appreciated" to Reliance. No security clearance or spectrum decision yet. Villages where fiber never reached have the most to gain when it opens.

Earnings week starts Tuesday.

posts.name: James Cat
posts.text:
Just over 400 Tesla Robotaxi vehicles in Tesla's Austin Robotaxi fleet, of which there appear to be ~360 active (90%). Operating hours of 6 AM to Midnight covering 18 hrs/day, or ~6.5k total car hours per day.

I estimate that to cover 100% of the Austin rideshare market at traditional rideshare pricing (which is what they are doing now), Tesla would need only 3,000 robotaxis operating 24 hours/day if 100% are active or 4,445 robotaxis at 90% utilization operating 18 hours/day.

As Tesla's fleet size increases, we need to observe what competitors do and how Tesla reacts. What happens in Austin will give us very good insights on how we can forecast the evolution of robotaxi and its economics in other markets. $TSLA

Tesla’s biggest moves in 2026 so far

May: Built the last Model S and Model X. Fremont line converted for Optimus.

July: Model Y L (six-seat) launched in the US. FSD subscriptions hit 1.48 million in Q2, biggest quarterly add ever.

Summer/Fall: Unsupervised Robotaxi expanded across Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. Optimus ramped to hundreds a week on old S/X line.

September: Cybercab (no wheel, no pedals) entered paid service in Austin and scaled past 300 units. Semi high-volume production started at the dedicated Nevada plant, customer deliveries underway.

October: Supercharger network passed 85,000 stalls with record Q3 usage. Powerwall VPP in California set a new record (85k+ homes, 600+ MW). Q3 deliveries of 486k. New flying Roadster demo.

posts.name: MoneyMarshal
posts.text:
財報前兩天，$TSLA 分析師都在算 EPS。

我這幾天卻一直在看另一個數字：

付費無人里程。

不是因為我忽然變得多懂自動駕駛。

是因為這條線，我盯了很多年，也失望過很多次。

二季電話會：超過 38 萬英里。

9 月 3 日 Cybercab 活動：超過 100 萬。

有人順著這個斜率推：到 10 月 21 日財報日，可能已經做到 200 萬到 300 萬英里——大約每週還在跑超過 20 萬英里。

這種斜率，我學乖了，不敢全信。

馬斯克畫過的餅，我吃過不止一次。

但這次有一點不一樣：

這不是簡報上的預測，是已經在跑的里程。

這不是財報附註裡的裝飾數字。

是投資人進電話會前，心裡那把尺。

所以這次財報，我真正想聽的不是 EPS。

是電話會。

更直白一點：股價更可能跟著電話會走，而不是跟著那一季 EPS 走。

有人寫調整後 EPS 約 0.42、共識約 0.45——差距不大。

市場要聽的，是 robotaxi 與 Optimus。

這幾年我看著別的板塊輪流漲，$TSLA 常常不動。

不是因為故事不夠，是因為故事一直沒兌現。

但偶爾，會有那麼一兩次，東西真的從簡報裡走出來，開始在路上跑。

那種時刻，就是你繼續留在這裡的原因。

除了里程，電話會上還有幾件事，我猜會被追問。

斯洛伐克已批准 FSD（歐洲品牌名 Tesla Assisted Driving），預期很快開推——歐洲地圖上，又多開了一扇小門。

NHTSA 則在審校區超速請願，以及 Cybercab 是否符合 FMVSS 自我認證——還沒正式調查，但會變成電話會上的兩道問號。

這種監管問句，這幾年我聽過太多次。

有些最後沒事，有些拖了很久。

Austin 那頭，有人寫 30 天內車隊增到超過 300 輛、累計無監督英里已過 100 萬——像一夜之間，停車場突然多出一整排會自己跑的車。

Dallas Cybercab「很快」上線，還沒給正式日期。

這些年我學到一件事：

馬斯克的故事，通常先遲到，再突然到。

所以我現在的判斷是：

10 月 21 日那天，數字可能只是開場白。

真正定調的，是這條里程線有沒有繼續往上爬，以及管理層怎麼講下一城、下一版軟體。

你呢？你會先看里程，還是先看監管？

posts.name: Marc Gravely
posts.text:
On August 5, a privately funded nuclear reactor switched on for the first time on a ranch outside Lockhart, Texas.

It went from bare ground to a working reactor in about 11 months.

It's a small test reactor for medical isotopes, the radioactive materials hospitals use to find and treat cancer.

Reactors make them by firing neutrons at target materials.

America has imported the most widely used one for decades, and this reactor is proving the process for bigger plants here.

Of the reactors in a new Department of Energy program that lets building run alongside the safety review, it's the first on private land.

The ranch is Proto-Town a hardware campus:

Companies building machines get workshops, open land to test on and somewhere to live, all on one site.

About a dozen are there now, working on driverless bulldozers, heavy-lift drones and robot-built homes.

Two Duke friends, @joshuafarahzad and @MerleNye, started it in 2024 while sleeping in a school bus on the site.

In 2025 Caldwell County exempted the ranch from any future county building rules.

The reactor still needed federal safety approval, and got it from the Department of Energy.

In 2022, this same land was the proposed site for Micron's $100 billion chip plant. Micron chose New York.

Four years later, there's a working nuclear reactor on it.

ARK Invest lays out their Bear, Base, and Bull Case for Tesla in their latest report - Here's what's notable for Robotaxi 📈

ARK says Robotaxi could be ~80% of Tesla's value by 2031 📊

By 2031:

💰 Base case: ~$4,400/share (bear $3,300, bull $5,000)

🚕 8.1M robotaxis deployed (bear 4.8M, bull 10M)

💸 $753B in ride-hail revenue, 52% of Tesla's total revenue of $1.45T (base case)

📈 Base case, Robotaxi alone is valued at $13.3T of a $16.4T enterprise value

🧐 Robotaxi's share is down from ~90% of Tesla's valuation in ARK's 2024 model, mainly because Optimus now holds a much larger valuation at $2.29T

Tesla Robotaxi has already logged 1M+ driverless miles, just ~7 months after public driverless rides began:

🚕 Tesla: ~7 months
🚙 Waymo: ~28 months
🚙 Zoox: ~34 months

What ARK's Tesla model leaves out (and its biggest risk):

🔴 No China Robotaxi operations
🟡 No surge pricing (left out to stay conservative)
🔴 Biggest risk per ARK: a slower ramp from regulatory delays or a shock event

How accurate have ARK's Tesla Robotaxi calls been?:

❌ 2021: Gave 50% odds of full autonomy by 2025. Actual 2025 ride-hail revenue: ~$0, per ARK

❌ 2023: Its bull scenarios assumed a Q4 2023 launch. Didn't happen.

✅ 2024: Called a 2025 launch. Tesla launched in Austin in June 2025

🎯 2026: Now projects 8.1M robotaxis by 2031

🟡 Their 2021 model targeted $3,000 for 2025 (~$1,000 split-adjusted). ARK's own table lists TSLA at $450 for 2025

ARK finally nailed a launch date in their 2024 report, but this report admits Robotaxi progress has been slower than expected (buried in their Optimus timeline, which they say was informed partly by the "slower-than-expected rate of Tesla's robotaxi progress") ✍️

ARK says its own model reflects a long-term positive bias on Tesla. As always, ARK is bullish, so I like to add some conservatism in their projected share price for 2031 ✍️

posts.name: JC Christopher
posts.text:
The day after the last $TSLA  earnings call, the stock fell through the floor. One hour before the call the stock was at $370, within 18 hours it was at $315, and within less than a week it was at $298. 

Although top-line revenue and deliveries had beaten expectations, FSD subscriptions were growing significantly, Robotaxi was making progress, and Cybercab was entering production, the story was fear.

Fear of historically large capex resulting in negative free cash flow, lower margins and lower ASPs, and a sense that investors were left unnerved from their perceived lack of a clear near-term timeline for when the heavy AI spend would improve margins and cash flow.

I have taken in a lot of information on this platform about Tesla over the past three months, as well as listened to some amazing folks in Spaces, and my take is that this quarter will be different, perhaps exactly the opposite.

You can only be shocked one time by a large capex number, and that definitely happened last quarter. Folks will see it again, but I don't believe it's going to have the same impact, it's part of the story now. And investors have seen similar from other larger hyperscalers. So I think the capex/free cash flow narrative is baked in now. 

I saw some great posts about deliveries and mix, and the smart folks are saying they believe ASPs will be up this quarter. Based on what I have seen and heard anecdotely, I agree with them. There should be margin improvement this quarter.

And there can be no mistake about Cybercab and Robotaxi now. If you are a TSLA investor and stay up with the company, all you have seen over the past month is Cybercabs flooding the streets of Austin, and meeting demand during busy seasons of X Takeover and ACL. We also know that Cybercab is gearing up to enter the network in other Texas cities soon. Folks will definitely want to hear about other locations where Robotaxi has either not yet scaled or where they previously stated they would be, but aren't yet; but this past month in Austin put to rest any potential questions about whether the hardware or software would work and scale. Finally, I get the sense that FSD subscriptions are going to see another significant tick up. 

TSLA the stock has regained literally everything it lost in that week after the Q2 call, over the past 3 months. And I don't believe we are going to see a repeat, in fact I feel more bullish about where we are going into this call than I have in a while.

Just please Tesla, don't mention anything about cats during the call......

posts.name: Ming
posts.text:
BOOOM 🚨 $TSLA's Q3 2026 update is out. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.48, ahead of the roughly $0.43 to $0.45 analysts expected 🔥

But the most revealing parts of the deck have little to do with EPS. They show a company steadily shifting its weight from cars to robots, robotaxis, and AI 🔥

🧠 FSD is now on more than three out of four new cars in North America.

Over 75% of new North American deliveries included FSD in Q3, up nearly 20 percentage points from Q2. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million, up from 1.48 million last quarter and 1.04 million a year ago. That count includes both upfront purchases and monthly subscriptions, and it leaves out free trials.

Europe is opening up too. Croatia, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia have approved FSD (Supervised) since the end of Q2, bringing the total to nine EU countries. More than 100,000 European customers have already driven over 160 million kilometers on it, or nearly 100 million miles.

Tesla says FSD subscriptions helped lift revenue and that FSD is driving demand wherever it's available. Put those together, and software is becoming a real revenue stream that can grow across the cars already on the road, not just with new sales. The outlook points the same way, with Tesla expecting hardware profits to be joined by faster growth in SI, software, and fleet-based profits.

🤖 Optimus has moved from prototypes to a real production line.

Optimus production has started on Tesla's high-volume lines in Fremont. The bots coming off that line are the first production-quality Optimus units Tesla has ever built, and Tesla says it has proven the current process is ready for a commercial product.

The capacity table lists Fremont as "Early Ramp" and shows a second Optimus site already under construction in Texas. Tesla hasn't shared a capacity number for either one yet.

This is the jump from prototypes to manufactured units, and that's the step that matters most for bringing costs down. Building a second site before the first one has even ramped suggests Tesla expects demand well beyond what Fremont can handle. The missing capacity figure is a reminder that the ramp is still early.

🚕 Cybercab is now giving rides in Austin, and unsupervised miles are growing fast.

Tesla started Robotaxi rides with Cybercab in Austin on September 3. By the end of the quarter, the Robotaxi service had logged nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles, eight times the total from three months earlier. Austin service now runs from 6am to midnight.

Texas now shows more than 125,000 units of installed annual Cybercab capacity with "Production" status. Tesla points out that installed capacity isn't the same as the current production rate, and it says battery supply is still the main constraint on vehicle volumes. It's ramping 4680 cells specifically to support Cybercab and Semi.

There's also a telling line in the outlook. Tesla says deliveries will depend partly on "allocation decisions between sale to customers and use for our owned and operated fleet." In plain English, Tesla is openly weighing how many cars to keep for its own network instead of selling them.

With the tooling listed as in production, batteries look like what will set the pace for Cybercab. Inside the car, riders get Grok with voice access to their inbox, calendar, files, and tasks, and Tesla pitches the cabin as "a second living room." Tesla is clearly thinking about what riders do during the trip, not just the trip itself.

⚡ Tesla plans to grow its AI training compute by about 50% in a single quarter.

Cortex 1 and Cortex 2 in Texas are rated at more than 105 MW and 120 MW, and Tesla has another 40 MW of compute on top of that, for roughly 265 MW in total. The goal is 400 MW by the end of the year, and Tesla says this compute trains autonomy software for both its vehicles and its humanoid robots.

Tesla is also building its own chip fab in Austin and plans to start commissioning equipment there in 2027. It hasn't said yet which chips the fab will make.

All of this shows up in the spending. R&D rose to $2.76 billion, up 69% from a year ago, and capex hit $4.73 billion, more than double last year's $2.25 billion. Even so, free cash flow stayed positive at $1.5 billion, and cash grew to $45.4 billion.

Because one compute pool trains both FSD and Optimus, progress on one can feed the other. A chip fab is one of the boldest vertical integration moves Tesla has made, and staying cash-positive while building it makes that bet much easier to fund.

🔭 Tesla is building every piece of its next chapter at the same time.

Robots are coming off a production line, driverless Cybercabs are carrying riders, FSD is turning into recurring software revenue, and the compute behind all of it is about to grow by half. Each piece makes the others stronger, and together they point to a Tesla whose future depends less on how many cars it sells and more on what its AI can do.

Growth is back at Tesla. Huge congrats to the entire team on an incredible quarter! 👏 

This what stands out to me from $TSLA Q3: 

THE FINANCIALS

• Revenue: $28.0B, roughly flat year over year.
• EPS: $0.48 vs. $0.45 expected.
• Gross margin: 19.6%, up from 18.0% a year ago and comfortably above the 17.9% Wall Street expected.
• Automotive gross margin excluding credits: 18.1%, up from 15.4%. Regulatory credit revenue fell from $417M to $113M. The underlying car business is getting more profitable.
• Free cash flow: POSITIVE $1.5B. Wall Street expected NEGATIVE $4.5B! 
• Cash pile: $45.4B, up 9%.

CARS

• Production rose +4% to 464,391 vehicles.
• Largest vehicle backlog in four years, with battery supply now the main constraint on more deliveries.
• Record deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan.
• Record production at Giga Berlin.
• Tesla built its 10 millionth vehicle.

FSD

• 1.74M active subscriptions, up 67% in a year.
• More than 75% of new cars in North America now come with FSD, up nearly 20 percentage points in a single quarter.
• Live in nine EU countries, with 100K+ customers and 160M+ kilometers driven.

ROBOTAXI

• Cybercab has been giving rides in Austin since September 3.
• Nearly 2M unsupervised miles, up 8x in one quarter.
• Austin service now runs from 6 a.m. to midnight.
• Grok is inside Cybercab, letting you handle email, your calendar and tasks by voice while you ride.

OPTIMUS

• Production has started on the high-volume lines in Fremont, building Tesla’s first production-quality robots.

SEMI

• Now in volume production.
• 500 miles of range at 82,000 lbs total weight, using roughly one-third the energy of a diesel truck.

ENERGY

• 13.7 GWh deployed, up 10%.
• Record order rate and backlog.
• Megafactory Texas is up and running, producing Megapacks.
• First Megapacks built using only Tesla’s own LFP cells.

AI COMPUTE

• Targeting 400 MW of training compute by year-end.
• Equipment installation at the Austin chip fab is planned to begin in 2027.

The tradeoff of all this is that operating income fell to $718M as Tesla increased spending on AI R&D. That’s a real cost today, but I’m comfortable with Tesla investing in the future. 

Underneath the flat revenue headline we may see from news outlets, FSD subscriptions are growing, Robotaxi is expanding, energy orders are at a record, and Optimus and Semi are entering production. Meanwhile, the vehicle backlog is the largest it’s been in four years.

It looks like to me the next leg of Tesla’s growth is taking shape right in front of us!

posts.text:
Things are coming together at Tesla, and I feel really good about where this company is headed. Today’s Q3 call gave me more confidence that the years of hard work the Tesla team has put in are beginning to pay off.

“I think we’re now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth.” - Elon Musk

This is what stands out to me the most from $TSLA Q3 2026.

FINANCIALS

• Revenue was $28.0B, flat YoY
• Adjusted EPS was $0.48 vs $0.45 expected
• Gross margin improved to 19.6% from 16.8% in Q2

• Auto margin excluding credits rose to 18.1% from 16.3% in Q2, even as credit revenue fell to $113M from $417M a year ago

• Free cash flow swung from -$1.09B in Q2 to +$1.53B
• Cash and investments reached $45.4B (lower spending and cash timing helped here, so the improvement wasn’t all from profit fyi)

• 2026 capex guidance is now ~$20B. 
• Tesla also secured $30B in borrowing capacity, with no planned draws this year.

CARS & FSD

“Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It’s exceeding our production by a significant margin.” - Elon Musk

• Deliveries were 486,532, down 2% YoY, but Tesla ended Q3 with its biggest passenger-car backlog in four years as battery supply remains the main production constraint today

• Paid FSD users reached 1.74M, up 67% YoY

• Over 75% of new North American deliveries included a paid FSD sign-up, versus over 55% in Q2

FYI, user count includes upfront buyers and monthly subscribers, with free trials excluded so half are now subscribers.

To me, FSD is becoming a bigger reason people buy a Tesla, with subscription income continuing after the sale. Elon hopes for EU-wide approval by Q1 2027, but for now, regulators control the timing.

CYBERCAB / ROBOTAXI

• Cybercab rides started September 3 in Austin and Elon mentioned that its Austin fleet has grown 10x since launch

• Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles grew 8x during Q3 to nearly 2M

• Ashok pointed to Dallas in November, while Tesla is targeting 24/7 service, highways and more weather conditions by year-end

• Lars is trying to get the first Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026. Separately, Ashok expects the first customer-owned cars to join the Robotaxi fleet around Q2 2027.

• Management expects Robotaxi to become noticeable financially around Q2 2027 and potentially a “big deal” by Q3/Q4 2027.

This is the opportunity I’m watching… vehicles earning $ revenue ride after ride, with costs improving as the service grows.

OPTIMUS

• Early production has started in Fremont, with a second factory under construction in Austin

• Elon expects deliveries to outside companies around the end of 2027, starting with industrial, dangerous and repetitive work. He expects at least a year, possibly longer, to reach roughly 20,000 robots a week.

ENERGY & OTHER THINGS

“We’re actually almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027.” - Elon Musk

• Storage deployments reached 13.7 GWh, up 10% YoY
• Megafactory Texas started production 
• Energy revenue fell 16%, and tariff refunds and warranty adjustments helped margins, so the backlog and production ramp matter most to me.
• Semi is in volume production. 
• Tesla is targeting roughly 5M vehicles a year by 2030, with volume chip production an aspiration for 2028.
• Elon called the Roadster demo “arguably the coolest demo of any product ever”... I was there, and I agree.

MY TAKE

What excites me is how many ways Tesla can grow… FSD subscriptions, Robotaxi rides, energy storage and eventually Optimus. 

I’ve believed in this for years.

I couldn’t care less what the stock does tomorrow or next week. What matters to me is Tesla building better products, growing the business and delivering on its long-term vision.

Growth is back at Tesla, imo, and I think the most exciting years are still ahead.

Congrats to the entire Tesla team!

posts.text:
MARKET IS COMPLETELY MISSING $TSLA ROBOTAXI INFLECTION POINT

Market is overlooking what could become the most important inflection point in Tesla's history because investors remain so focused on deteriorating automotive profitability that they're missing how quickly Tesla is moving toward commercializing autonomy across its existing vehicle ecosystem but on the surface Q3 earnings certainly weren't impressive for a company commanding a valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion, with revenue essentially flat at $28 billion, vehicle deliveries declining 2% YoY and operating income falling 56% to approximately $718 million as R&D spending continued accelerating. 

Those are legitimate concerns especially when the market is already assigning substantial value to businesses that haven't reached commercial scale but automotive gross margins excluding regulatory credits improved to 18.1%, vehicle deliveries exceeded expectations and management reported its highest automotive backlog in four years but I think the bigger story is that Tesla's existing automotive business is increasingly becoming the distribution platform for something potentially much more valuable which is a recurring software and autonomous transportation ecosystem that could eventually generate revenue long after the original vehicle sale.

The clearest evidence of that transition came from FSD adoption because Tesla's North American attach rate surged to 75% of new vehicle deliveries from 55% in Q2 while active FSD subscriptions reached approximately 1.74 million, growing 67% YoY and I think those are among most important numbers Tesla has reported this year because they suggest that consumers are increasingly engaging with autonomy software rather than simply purchasing vehicles for transportation. 

Tesla now has an installed base exceeding 10 million vehicles, and every additional customer adopting FSD creates an opportunity to generate recurring software revenue without manufacturing another car. Of course, attach rates don't necessarily translate directly into permanent paying subscribers, especially when promotional trials are involved but the direction of adoption is encouraging. 

What makes this interesting is that Tesla is building these software relationships on top of an existing global distribution network, which potentially lowers customer acquisition costs while creating higher margin revenue opportunities. I think investors are still underestimating how much the economics of Tesla could change if software revenue begins representing a meaningfully larger percentage of total automotive revenue rather than remaining a relatively small contributor to the broader business which brings me to Robotaxi because I think we're finally approaching the stage where Tesla's autonomy ambitions need to be evaluated through actual commercial deployment rather than demonstrations and promises about what the technology could eventually accomplish. 

Tesla began offering Cybercab rides in Austin during September, while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles reportedly increased eightfold sequentially, providing early evidence that its autonomous transportation network is beginning to expand because the significance here isn't simply that Tesla can manufacture a vehicle capable of driving without a human operator, but that a commercially successful Robotaxi network could fundamentally change the revenue generated by each vehicle over its useful life. 

Instead of recognizing revenue primarily when a customer purchases a car, Tesla could eventually generate recurring revenue every time an autonomous vehicle transports a passenger, with the economics improving as fleet utilization increases and operating costs decline which is why I think the biggest disconnect in Tesla comes from investors evaluating the company primarily on the profitability of its automotive business today while struggling to determine how much value its autonomy, robotics and energy businesses could eventually generate. 

My thesis is that Tesla's Robotaxi moment is beginning to arrive, but the real opportunity will only become clear once management demonstrates that autonomous vehicles can operate safely, attract consistent paying demand and generate attractive returns at scale and if Tesla succeeds I think the market could eventually value the company very differently from how it values the automotive business today, and that's why I'm paying considerably more attention to the trajectory of FSD adoption and Robotaxi commercialization than whether automotive revenue grows a few percentage points next quarter.

Tesla's earnings calls have felt flat vs SpaceX, but the growth and strategy behind Robotaxi are anything but 🧐

🤖 Vision-only Robotaxis were once an unproven technical risk, but skepticism is being silenced. While that risk is mitigated with every unsupervised mile, regulatory risk is the next hurdle to scaling.

🛠️ Once the regulatory risk is handled, Tesla's edge is cost and efficiency - their engineering prowess, regional factories, and vertical integration allow them to make the lowest cost product with the best customer experience while iterating on fleet and vehicle efficiencies to ultimately drive competitors out.

📈 Tesla has been testing their scaling strategy in both breadth and depth for the past year - open 6 cities in a short period of time, and flood 1 city with Robotaxis (Austin). This is to improve both strategies simultaneously so they can execute each at a larger scale over time.

🔍 It took 3-5 years of flat calls and empty promises before preparation met opportunity. It is understandable to feel the ramp is moving slowly, but we are still in the early innings. Ashok said it himself: "…you're seeing the result of many years of work, it didn't just happen in the last several months."

posts.name: Ming
posts.text:
BOOM 🚨 Tesla just dropped its first-ever Robotaxi Safety Report—and the early data is looking impressive 🔥

Between January 22 and October 18, 2026, Tesla’s driverless fleet logged over 3.11 million miles (5.01 million km) across six U.S. cities without a single safety driver behind the wheel.

The standout takeaways:
🎖️ 0 injuries in collisions where the Robotaxi made first contact. 
🎖️ 0 airbag deployments. 
🎖️ 0 pedestrians or cyclists struck in first-contact incidents.

These weren't easy, low-stress miles under sunny skies, either. The fleet took on real-world edge cases:
✅ 862,000+ miles after dark 
✅ 575,000+ miles in peak rush-hour gridlock 
✅ 113,000+ miles in the pouring rain

Here’s where the numbers get really interesting.

Benchmarking against local police crash data across Austin, Dallas, and Houston, Tesla estimates average human drivers covering that exact same ~2.95 million miles would have chalked up:
⚠️ 9.1 injury crashes 
⚠️ 4.1 crashes with airbag deployments 
⚠️ 0.52 collisions involving pedestrians or cyclists

(A key caveat: Tesla’s pedestrian and injury metrics specifically track collisions where the Robotaxi initiated contact, whereas the human benchmark tallies crashes regardless of who made first contact. It’s not an exact apples-to-apples comparison, but the margin remains eye-opening.)

Meanwhile, the operational footprint is scaling fast:
✅ Austin leads the pack with over 2.1 million miles 
✅ Dallas sits at 608,000+ miles, with Houston crossing 226,000 miles 
✅ Driverless operations are already live in Orlando, Tampa, and Miami 
✅ Next in line: Las Vegas, Phoenix, Jacksonville, and San Antonio

Beyond the headline numbers, the biggest win here might be transparency. 

Tesla published its full safety methodology alongside downloadable, raw NHTSA collision filings, giving the public an unvarnished look at how the tech actually performs in the wild.

Granted, 3.11 million miles is still Chapter 1. Validating autonomy at true commercial scale will take tens of millions more miles across every season, weather pattern, and road type imaginable.

Still, the early benchmark is remarkably strong—and the road to mass driverless mobility just got a whole lot more exciting 🔥

Tham vọng robotaxi của Tesla còn phụ thuộc vào rào cản pháp lý và tiến độ thương mại hóa.

Elon Musk cho biết Tesla đang đặt cược vào mảng xe tự lái với mục tiêu đảm nhiệm hơn một nửa nhu cầu đi lại của hành khách trên toàn cầu. Tuy vậy, tham vọng này vẫn phụ thuộc lớn vào rào cản pháp lý tại từng quốc gia và tiến độ thương mại hóa công nghệ.

Theo Tesla và truyền thông quốc tế ngày 22/10 ), tại cuộc gọi công bố kết quả kinh doanh hôm 21/10, Musk nói rằng nếu xe tự lái được phép vận hành rộng rãi tại các thị trường liên quan, Tesla có thể đảm nhiệm hơn một nửa tổng quãng đường di chuyển của hành khách trên thế giới.

Musk cho rằng các quy định tại nước ngoài, đặc biệt khi gắn với mục tiêu bảo hộ ngành công nghiệp nội địa, có thể cản trở kế hoạch mở rộng toàn cầu của Tesla. Nhận định lần này cũng táo bạo hơn dự báo ông đưa ra trong cuộc họp công bố kết quả kinh doanh hồi tháng 1, khi nói rằng phần lớn hoạt động di chuyển rồi sẽ chuyển sang xe tự lái và tỷ lệ quãng đường do con người trực tiếp cầm lái sẽ giảm xuống dưới 5%. Khi đó, Waymo, Zoox, Ford, General Motors (GM) và Rivian được nhắc đến như những đối thủ trên thị trường tự lái.

Kỳ vọng vào xe tự lái hiện là một trong những trụ cột chính trong câu chuyện định giá Tesla. Về dài hạn, hãng cho biết chỉ giữ lại Roadster - mẫu xe thể thao giá cao - như một trong số ít dòng xe vẫn cần người lái trực tiếp điều khiển. Tháng 9, Tesla ra mắt mẫu robotaxi không vô lăng Cybercab tại Texas nhằm mở rộng tham vọng ở mảng gọi xe. Công ty cũng chuẩn bị triển khai dịch vụ tại Florida, song Cơ quan An toàn Giao thông Đường cao tốc Quốc gia Mỹ (NHTSA) đã mở cuộc điều tra ngay sau khi Cybercab ra mắt để xem xét quy trình tự chứng nhận của mẫu xe này.

Một sức ép khác với Tesla là việc nhiều lần lỡ hẹn với các mốc triển khai xe tự lái. Musk từng dự báo công nghệ tự lái không cần tài xế giám sát sẽ được mở rộng trên toàn nước Mỹ vào năm 2025, nhưng mục tiêu này đến nay vẫn chưa hoàn thành. Tại cuộc gọi công bố kết quả kinh doanh mới nhất, Ashok Elluswamy, Phó chủ tịch phụ trách trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) của Tesla, cho biết tính năng Full Self-Driving (FSD) không cần giám sát có thể được triển khai trên một số xe của khách hàng sớm nhất vào khoảng quý II/2027 để đưa vào vận hành robotaxi.

Để kịch bản Tesla nắm giữ phần lớn thị trường đi lại của hành khách toàn cầu trở thành hiện thực, hãng không chỉ phải hoàn thiện công nghệ mà còn cần được phê duyệt về mặt pháp lý, mở rộng dịch vụ và bám sát tiến độ thương mại hóa. Bất chấp sự tự tin của Musk, lợi thế cạnh tranh thực sự của Tesla sẽ còn phụ thuộc vào tốc độ mở rộng dịch vụ xe tự lái và khả năng chứng minh hiệu quả công nghệ trong thời gian tới.

Theo Seung-ah Yoo

posts.name: Shawn
posts.text:
🚨 Tesla Robotaxi：下一步不是增加车辆，而是寻找乘客！

10月23日，Tesla Robotaxi 在 Austin 再次扩张，服务区域增加约10%，向东南延伸至F1美洲赛道周边，运营时间也延长至凌晨1点。

但这次扩张有一个值得注意的细节：新增区域并非人口密集区，而是人口相对稀疏的郊区。

为什么Tesla要向这里扩张？

我的判断是：Austin现有Robotaxi车队可能已经拥有足够运力，Tesla正在主动寻找更多需求。

本周末的F1美国大奖赛恰好提供了大量潜在乘客，Tesla显然不想错过这个机会。

但F1带来的只是短期需求。赛事结束后，日常订单能否支撑不断扩大的车队，才是真正的考验。

Robotaxi商业化可能正在进入一个新阶段：从解决供给问题，转向解决需求问题。

当然，目前还没有足够的订单数据证明Austin已经出现运力过剩。

不过，华尔街接下来应该关注的，不再仅仅是Austin有多少辆Robotaxi，而是：

每辆车每天完成多少订单？每单贡献多少利润？

这两个数字，才是决定Robotaxi商业价值的关键。

#Tesla #Robotaxi #TSLA

Tesla's Cybercab just got a regulatory tailwind

NHTSA proposed changes to the federal vehicle lighting standard for driverless cars

Vehicles with no manual controls would no longer need physical hazard switches, beam shifters or turn signal levers

It also sets a standard for optional cyan exterior lights that show when the self-driving system is in control

The proposal publishes in the Federal Register on Oct 26, as part of DOT's push to make cars without steering wheels or pedals easier to build and sell

Cybercab of course has no steering wheel, no pedals and no mirrors

NHTSA did open an audit query last month into how Cybercab was certified, but the rules are now being rewritten around EXACTLY the kind of vehicle Tesla is building

特斯拉的FSD的里程碑——德州Robotxi 实现L4认证

        德州已授权特斯拉Robotaxi运营。根据2025年通过的德州参议院第2807号法案（SB 2807），商业自动驾驶车辆需获得德州机动车管理局（TxDMV）的授权。该规定自2026年5月28日起强制执行。特斯拉通过自我认证方式，将其Robotaxi（包括Model Y和Cybercab）申报为SAE Level 4，并获得了TxDMV的授权。

目前情况大致如下：
         特斯拉已在德州注册并运营数百辆Robotaxi车辆（包括大量Cybercab），车队规模持续扩大。
         奥斯汀已开放Cybercab公开叫车服务（2026年9月初起）。
          德州采用自我认证模式：TxDMV不进行独立测试，由运营商自行声明符合要求；如有问题，可追究责任。
          需要注意的是，这是州级运营授权，不等于联邦层面全面认可。美国国家公路交通安全管理局（NHTSA）仍在审查Cybercab（无方向盘、无踏板）的联邦安全标准合规性。

         简单说：德州已正式放行特斯拉Robotaxi商业运营，车队在快速扩张中。

Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet utilization (unsupervised miles per day per vehicle) has risen steadily since July, from the low-40s to the low-100s today.

We estimated this by combining Texas DMV registrations (Cybercab + Model Y) with Florida vehicle counts from public trackers, then dividing the reported unsupervised mileage growth by the fleet size.

Mileage is compounding faster than the fleet is expanding, meaning the cars already on the road are being used more intensively.

Even so, utilization is still well below Waymo’s typical 200 miles per day per vehicle, so Tesla has substantial headroom to increase usage further as the network matures.

posts.name: James Cat
posts.text:
Due to regulation, Tesla's opportunity may lie more with focusing on geographic depth, and less with geographic reach.

For example, it will be easier for Tesla to penetrate deeper into the Robotaxi jurisdictions/territories it is already operating in (ex: Austin), than it will be for Tesla to rapidly expand into other states or countries where regulations have not yet been modernized. 

This offers several advantages for Tesla:

1. Focus. 

Tesla could narrow its training compute on mastery of fewer markets. In this scenario, it stands to reason that performance would improve in these focus regions more than they otherwise would if training capacity were instead distributed between more markets.

This would improve FSD performance, safety and help Tesla build evidence to support its government relations push to modernize regulation in other markets that are less welcoming to autonomous vehicles (Waymo's approach).

2. Learn Market Economics and Price Elasticities

In this more concentrated scenario, Tesla could flood these concentrated markets with an abundance of vehicles, and truly get a sense of what the economics need to be to displace ridesharing/personal vehicle ownership/public transit. How will consumers adopt the service? What will competitors do? How profitable is this strategy? Is this strategy scalable?

Tesla will need to reach a critical mass of vehicles and drive down price significantly before they could achieve this. These learnings can then be applied to other markets.

Given the challenges with regulation, Tesla may be forced into thinking this way (if they're not already). This could explain why Austin is being so heavily prioritized over Florida markets, or even other Texas markets. Tesla may already be thinking along these lines, today.

$TSLA

posts.name: Dovydas Vitkauskas
posts.text:
Amazon Zoox robotaxi, a Google Waymo car, and a Tesla Cybercab became trapped in a viral face-to-face standoff on a narrow city street in 🇺🇸Austin, Texas, showcasing a classic real-world artificial intelligence deadlock.

The vehicles met head-on on a narrow side street constricted by cars parked on both sides. Because each company programs its vehicles with proprietary decision-making algorithms, the vehicles struggled to establish right-of-way protocol without a human driver to initiate a courtesy gesture or negotiate positioning.

Eyewitnesses noted that the Waymo continued to creep aggressively forward instead of yielding. Meanwhile, the Tesla Cybercab - which runs entirely unsupervised on vision-based software without a steering wheel or pedals - was seen reversing to clear space for the others. 

Observers also pointed out that Zoox’s unique bidirectional carriage design makes native reversing straightforward, though both it and the Waymo remained locked in position for several minutes before traffic could clear. 

This event highlights a prominent operational barrier for autonomous fleets: multi-platform coordination. While current robotaxis excel at perception and safety when interacting with fixed obstacles or rule-following humans, they struggle when they encounter another AI entity governed by a completely different set of non-standardized routing protocols. Similar standoffs between Zoox and Waymo vehicles have previously been documented in San Francisco, indicating that “algorithm clashes” are becoming a frequent consequence of multi-fleet urban deployments. 

Can the robotaxi companies program “courtesy gestures” as part of their algorithms?

If Tesla’s Robotaxi Miles Keep Compounding at 20% a Week, the Math Gets Interesting Fast | Paul Fosse, CleanTechnica

Tesla just passed Waymo in Austin in weekly driverless miles. If its recent 20% weekly growth holds, it passes Waymo nationally in roughly 11 weeks and is doing the volume of Uber + Lyft across three Texas metros by mid-February.

The accumulating unsupervised miles are already large enough to start answering the safety question versus humans and versus Waymo. That has implications for whether LiDAR is actually required.

I noted in my Q3 earnings summary that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxi miles jumped from 250,000 last quarter to about 1.7 million, and then the same day the company said they were already at 3.3 million. That implies roughly 20% weekly growth on the recent run. I want to take that number seriously for a limited window and see where it goes relative to Waymo and to the actual ride-hail market in the Texas cities where Tesla is already operating. Then I’ll draw some conclusions.

It looks like Tesla has already surpassed Waymo in Austin. Next, let’s look at what it would take for them to pass Waymo nationally and for them to start to eat into Uber and Lyft marketshare.

The Math Through the Crossovers

Tesla Unsupervised Weekly Miles Projection (20% compound weekly growth from current national unsupervised miles/week):

From 558K/week, the rate crosses Waymo’s recent ~4 million weekly national total in around week 11. By week 16, the weekly rate would be roughly 10 million miles. That is the point where Tesla’s weekly volume would exceed half the current Uber + Lyft volume in Austin, Dallas, and Houston combined.

How Fast Has Waymo Actually Been Growing?

Waymo’s recent numbers make the crossover more striking. Through the end of June 2026, the company had logged 271.3 million cumulative rider-only miles. In Q2 2026, it added only about 50.7 million miles, versus 49.9 million in Q1—sequential growth of roughly 1.6%. Earlier quarters in 2025 had seen quarterly growth of 15% or better. City-level data shows the same cooling: Phoenix has posted two straight quarterly declines, Austin’s quarter-over-quarter growth fell from over 100% early in 2025 to about 4% in Q2 2026, Los Angeles was near 9%, and San Francisco was near 13%. Atlanta grew faster off a small base, but the overall picture is a large installed base whose percentage growth has slowed sharply. Even if Waymo regains its quarterly growth of 15%, that is dramatically lower than the 970% quarterly growth implied in my table above.

Austin, Dallas, and Houston: The Realistic Near-Term Market

The Austin metro area has roughly 2.4–2.6 million people and about 45 million vehicle-miles traveled per day (roughly 315 million per week). Waymo’s recent weekly rate there is about 400,000 miles; Tesla’s most recent tracked week in Austin was about 438,000 miles. Both are still tiny fractions of total driving. Dallas–Fort Worth (~5.7 million people, ~157 million daily VMT) and Houston (~5.9 million people, ~144 million daily VMT) are substantially larger. Tesla’s current Dallas zone is already bigger than its early Austin footprint (roughly 81 square miles) and has logged over 600,000 cumulative unsupervised miles. Houston remains smaller: about 25 square miles and roughly 226,000 cumulative miles. Waymo is present in both cities with public service. Estimated weekly Uber + Lyft miles (combined, paid passenger miles only):

- Austin: 1.5–2.5 million
- Dallas–Fort Worth: 4–6 million
- Houston: 4–6 million
- Three-city total: roughly 10–14 million

Pricing Changes the Addressable Market

If Tesla prices at roughly half of Uber, the relevant market is no longer limited to ride-hail substitution. Personal driving in the three metros is hundreds of millions of miles per week. Even a 1–2% shift of trips that are currently driven privately becomes several million additional weekly miles once the per-mile cost drops well below the fully loaded cost of owning and operating a personal car for many trips. Some off-peak or transfer-heavy transit trips (CapMetro, DART, Metro) become competitive as well.

The practical near-to-medium-term opportunity in just these three cities is therefore larger than the 5–7 million weekly ride-hail slice—potentially 10–20+ million once personal-trip substitution appears. The 16-week 20% compounding path already reaches ~10 million weekly miles. That clears half the current Uber + Lyft total in the three cities and leaves room for the start of personal-trip substitution, provided the Dallas and Houston geofences expand enough and the fleet scales to absorb the demand. Sustaining 20% weekly for 16 straight weeks while also enlarging the service areas is the operational question, not the demand question. Price becomes the demand lever once the vehicles and the geofences are large enough.

What Could Go Wrong

The arithmetic is clean. The path from here is not.

First, the 20% weekly rate is a launch rate observed while the absolute numbers are still small and concentrated in one city. Sustaining it for 16 weeks means the weekly addition itself has to keep growing. That requires either rapid vehicle deployment or a sharp rise in utilization per vehicle. Both get harder as the fleet expands: charging infrastructure has to keep pace, maintenance capacity has to scale, and local regulators have to approve larger operating zones. A single high-profile incident that triggers a pause in any of the three cities would flatten the curve immediately.

Second, geofence expansion is not automatic. Dallas and Houston currently operate in far smaller zones than Austin. Moving them to Austin-scale coverage involves mapping, local permits, and public acceptance. Any delay pushes the volume absorption problem into 2027.

Third, utilization can fall even if the fleet grows. If vehicles spend more time empty, charging, or waiting for demand that has not yet shifted from personal cars, the miles per vehicle drop and the required fleet size rises.

Fourth, pricing at half of Uber’s price assumes Tesla can still cover its costs at that level. If insurance, remote assistance, or cleaning costs run higher than expected, the price cut either shrinks or disappears, and the personal-trip substitution story weakens.

None of these are fatal. They are the ordinary constraints that turn an early exponential into an S-curve. The 16-week path clears the math for a material position relative to current ride-hail in three Texas cities. Whether the vehicles, the zones, and the operations arrive on that schedule is the open question.

My Read

Tesla is not primarily trying to out-mile Waymo on a percentage basis. It is trying to show that the unit economics of an unsupervised Cybercab (or Model Y) can work at scale, with revenue expected to become noticeable in 2027. The recent 20% weekly growth is the clearest signal yet that the software has cleared an internal quality bar in the cities where it is running—and the accumulating unsupervised miles already provide a meaningful basis to compare safety outcomes against both human drivers and Waymo. If Tesla’s rate of incidents continues to hold as the fleet scales, it undercuts the long-standing claim that LiDAR is required to operate more safely than humans.

Superior results relative to Waymo would further suggest that more capable software matters more than simply adding sensors to less sophisticated systems. Whether the same growth rate can be sustained long enough for the weekly total to pass Waymo’s, and whether Dallas and Houston can be brought up to Austin-like coverage in the next four months, are the next two questions. History suggests at least one constraint appears before the curve stays perfectly exponential, but the arithmetic no longer requires an absurd number of cities or an impossible fleet to become material relative to existing ride-hail. Any progress they make in Florida (my home state) in Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and Jacksonville is a bonus for the short term, but they need to continue their growth going forward.

Did you know that beating Uber, Lyft and Waymo is too small a goal for Tesla? And one number shows why 🔥

$TSLA’s Robotaxi is growing fast. Cybercabs have been giving paid rides in Austin since September, Dallas follows next month, and unsupervised miles grew eightfold last quarter.

So naturally, most people judge Tesla against those three rivals. The debate is usually about who has more cars, cheaper fares and more cities.

That’s the wrong scoreboard! The better question is how many miles Americans travel by car each year, and how many of those miles happen in a ride-hailing car at all.

The answer is surprisingly lopsided. For every mile Americans ride in an Uber, Lyft, Waymo or any other ride-hailing car, they drive about 70 miles in their own.

That’s the number that matters: 70 🔥

Picture all the miles Americans travel by car as a pizza cut into 71 slices. Ride-hailing gets one slice. The other 70 are driven by people behind the wheel of their own cars.

So the market Uber, Lyft and Waymo fight over is only a little over 1 percent of American driving. The real prize is everything else, and that's the market Tesla is going after.

Once you see that, a lot of Tesla's choices suddenly make sense: the 30-cents-per-mile target, the giant Cybercab production plans, and Elon's claim that Tesla will end up carrying most of the world's passenger miles.

🧮 WHERE THE 70 COMES FROM

America's cars, SUVs and pickups covered about 2.9 trillion miles in 2023, according to the Federal Highway Administration. That's 259 million vehicles averaging about 11,100 miles each.

A 70x gap puts ride-hailing at roughly 40 billion miles a year. Uber and Lyft's own commissioned study fits that scale. Even in six major metro areas where both services are popular, including San Francisco and Boston, the two companies made up just 1 to 3 percent of all miles driven. In other words, even in its strongest cities, ride-hailing only gets one or two slices of the pizza.

Ride-hailing changed how we get to the airport. It barely touched how America actually gets around.

💸 WHY RIDE-HAILING ONLY GETS ONE SLICE

The reason is price. A typical 5-mile UberX ride costs about $15 to $22 in most US cities this year. With fees included, that works out to roughly $3 to $4.40 per mile.

AAA's 2026 study puts the full cost of owning a new car at about 86 cents per mile. That figure counts depreciation, financing, fuel and maintenance.

When riding costs three to five times more than owning, people buy cars. They save ride-hailing for the airport, the bar and the occasional emergency. A big share of every fare pays the human behind the wheel, and that cost doesn't shrink with scale.

⚡ HOW 30 CENTS UNLOCKS THE OTHER 70

Tesla's target for its Robotaxi fleet is 30 cents per mile. On last week's Q3 call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said Tesla isn't there yet but sees a clear path as the fleet scales.

The trick isn't only removing the driver. The average American car drives about 30 miles a day and sits parked the rest of the time. A robotaxi working most of the day could plausibly cover 250 miles or more. That spreads the cost of one vehicle over eight or nine times as many miles, and that is how the price per mile collapses.

At 30 cents, riding becomes cheaper than owning, even with a healthy margin on top. That's when the other 70 slices finally come within reach.

This isn't about replacing the Tesla already in your garage, since each extra mile in a car you own costs very little. Elon said on the call that the Model 3, Model Y and Roadster remain the cars people will want to own, while Cybercab is mostly Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service. The real fight is over the next car someone decides whether to buy, especially the second one.

🏭 ONE SLICE VS. 70 SLICES

This is where the number gets wild. Suppose each robotaxi covers about 100,000 miles a year. Then the one slice ride-hailing serves today would need only around 400,000 vehicles.

On the Q3 call, Tesla said its Cybercab line in Texas has a listed capacity of more than 125,000 a year, and Lars Moravy added that the line can actually do significantly more. Even at the listed rate, that single line could build enough cars to cover all of today's US ride-hailing in about three years.

The other 70 slices would take closer to 29 million vehicles. At that same rate, one line would need more than two centuries to get there. Tesla's factory ambitions only make sense against that bigger market. Building a Cybercab line just to fight Uber would be like building a stadium for a dinner party.

🔮 THE REAL TARGET

On the call, Elon said Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth wherever it's allowed to operate freely.

Read next to the 70x gap, that isn't a ride-hailing prediction. Ride-hailing holds just one slice out of 71, so a majority can only come from the miles people drive themselves today.

For a century, owning a car has been the cheapest way to get door to door on your own schedule. At 30 cents a mile, that would no longer be true 🔥

posts.name: Teslaconomics
posts.text:
Just wondering... how many Tesla Cybercabs do you plan on owning? 

I’ve been running the numbers for a while, and I honestly think Cybercab could become one of the most exciting investment opportunities regular people have ever had. The idea of owning a car that earns money while I’m home with my family is something I can’t stop thinking about these days...

However, I know the numbers have to work. Here’s the scenario I’m working with, assuming I buy the car outright:

• Purchase price: about ~$30,000  
• Average fare: $1.35 per paid mile  
• Average paid miles: 150 a day across the full year  
• Tesla’s share: an assumed 30%

That works out to about $74,000 a year in fares. After Tesla’s assumed share, about $51,700 would be left before expenses. To keep roughly $30,000 a year, I’d need charging, cleaning, insurance, tires, maintenance and money set aside to eventually replace the car to fit within about $21,700.

If it holds, we’re talking about roughly ~$30,000 a year per cab before income tax. Under those assumptions, the car could earn back its purchase price in about a year, which is wild imo. 

At $30,000 in annual earnings per cab, here’s how many you’d need to reach at least these targets.

• $100K a year → 4 Cybercabs  
• $250K a year → 9 Cybercabs  
• $500K a year → 17 Cybercabs  
• $750K a year → 25 Cybercabs  
• $1M a year → 34 Cybercabs

I have to let this sink in... thirty-four cars, under these assumptions, could produce just over $1 million a year before income tax.

Of course, 34 cars would also be a real business to run. Like someone still has to handle cleaning, repairs, charging and all the things passengers manage to spill.

I keep comparing this potential with rental property, which I also own.

Buying rentals, especially here in the Bay Area, takes serious $ money. Then you have property taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancies and mortgage payments if you borrow. And occasionally, a late-night call about a broken toilet. Also takes a long time to make your $ back. 

In this Cybercab scenario, four cars would cost about $120,000 before taxes and setup, and could produce roughly $120,000 in just a year before income tax. That relationship between the $ money you put in and the income you get back is what makes owning a Cybercab, a major advantage.

I know there are tradeoffs too, of course... a property can rise in value. A car doing tens of thousands of miles a year wears out. A Cybercab may spare you the broken toilet, but it will probably still need more attention on a daily basis.

Also, one of the biggest question in my model is whether each Cybercab can consistently average 150 PAID miles a day. Driving empty to the next pickup adds costs without adding fare revenue. Charging, cleaning and repairs take time. And more competition could push fares even lower.

Despite these things, there is REAL progress to look at today. Cybercabs are already carrying paying riders in Austin and expanding, and Tesla has said it’s aiming to begin customer deliveries by the end of 2026. Tesla’s broader ride-hailing service now reaches parts of seven U.S. metro areas.

For me, I’d start with a couple of Cybercabs, see what they actually earn, and build toward a fleet of 25+ if the numbers hold up. I’m seriously excited for the day I get to send my own fleet out to work.

I believe it’s only a matter of time before Tesla becomes the #1 robotaxi provider in the U.S.

posts.name: Fred Lambert
posts.text:
Credit where it's due: Tesla's driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver's seat. A year ago, that wasn't the case.

But "never a real contest" is a strange thing to say when you're behind by 7x on weekly miles and 87x on cumulative miles, and your one win depends on comparing your newest week to your rival's data from last spring.

What stands out to us is the type of autonomy Tesla is deploying. In 2020, Musk wrote that "Waymo is impressive, but a highly specialized solution," and that Tesla's approach was "a general solution." For years, Tesla fans dismissed Waymo as a geofenced system that only worked in mapped areas with lots of restrictions.

Now look at Tesla's Robotaxi: geofenced, no highways, avoiding railroad crossings, taking 70 minutes for 10-minute trips, and limited by hours because the software isn't ready for anything with "the slightest possible risk." By Musk's own old definition, that's a highly specialized solution. Waymo is the one driving on freeways now.

Cybercab passes Model Y, easyJet picks Starlink and Ship 42 lights up. Tuesday in five lines:

• Tesla registered 81 new Cybercabs in Texas, so the robotaxi fleet is 1,051 with 544 Cybercabs and 507 Model Y.
That is 225 more Cybercabs since 9 Oct, and Texas is only one state.

• NASASpaceflight showed Ship 42 running a single-engine static fire at Massey's for Flight 15.
A small test, but every Starship flight starts with days like this.

• Elon quoted the What's New in Grok Bot video, with Pages, Vault, 1Password, Apple integrations, bots that make videos and X Spaces in the chapter list.
When Elon shares it, millions see it, and that list shows how fast it is moving.

• easyJet will put Starlink on its A320 and A321 planes, its first onboard Wi-Fi ever, from the first half of 2027 to early 2028.
After years with no Wi-Fi at all, easyJet goes straight to Starlink.

• AFRL recovered its cargo pods after the Starfall capsule splashed down in the Pacific.
The temperature, shock and vibration data is what counts, and AFRL's post gives no results yet.

A good day for anyone who likes to see things get built.

Creation is the most egalitarian act. When we all create we all benefit. Creation is within all of us, it's what make humans unique,  it's our duty to protect the privilege to do it. 

Have a blessed day

posts.text:
Elon Musk (@elonmusk) said Tesla’s ($TSLA) Robotaxi service will soon expand to include beaches in Miami and Tampa after Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called for broader coverage.

Tesla’s current Robotaxi geofences span roughly 31 square miles in Miami, 24 square miles in Tampa and 26 square miles in Orlando.

DeSantis said the Miami and Tampa service areas should include the beaches. Musk responded simply: “Coming soon.”

Tesla’s largest Robotaxi geofences remain in Texas, with Austin covering about 272 square miles and Houston around 254 square miles. Dallas covers roughly 81 square miles.

The planned Florida expansion would put Tesla into closer competition with Alphabet’s ($GOOGL) Waymo, which already operates across larger service areas in Miami and Tampa that include beach zones.

Tesla is also expanding its Cybercab fleet. Recent registration data cited by investor Sawyer Merritt showed 544 Cybercabs registered for Robotaxi service in Texas, surpassing 507 Model Y vehicles.

That brings Tesla’s registered Robotaxi fleet in Austin to more than 1,000 vehicles across Cybercab and Model Y.

ARK Invest’s Cathie Wood remains highly bullish on the opportunity, arguing that Robotaxis could eventually account for more than 80% of Tesla’s enterprise value.

Critics such as Ross Gerber have questioned the pace of Tesla’s rollout, especially as competitors including Waymo and Amazon’s ($AMZN) Zoox continue expanding into new markets.

posts.name: Ming
posts.text:
Dear Mr. Anderson,

Tesla never ignored physics.

I'm writing because of what you told The Verge on October 27, when you called dropping radar from a self-driving car "a weird religious stance that ignores physics." That line got a lot of attention among Tesla owners, and I think it deserves a direct answer.

You know this territory better than most. You ran Tesla's Autopilot program from late 2015 to late 2016, cofounded Aurora, and now lead product at GM.

Your new employer is betting the other way. A 2028 Cadillac Escalade IQ will launch eyes-off highway driving with cameras, radar and lidar all working together.

As I understand it, your case rests on four claims. Lidar helps camera systems learn faster, cameras can't see through dense fog, cameras can't measure instantaneous velocity the way radar can, and radar is so cheap that removing it makes no sense.

I agree that physics is real, and nobody at Tesla is pretending otherwise. What I'd like to show you is that Tesla's own engineering has been answering these exact points for years, and two of your arguments describe things Tesla already does.

A lot has also changed since you left. The in-house FSD computer arrived in 2019, camera-only Tesla Vision followed in 2021, and the end-to-end neural network that drives the car today came in 2024.

So let me take your physics one claim at a time.

🎓 ON LIDAR AS A TEACHER, TESLA HAS BEEN DOING THAT FOR YEARS

You said lidar works on a wavelength close to visible light, so it helps camera systems learn faster. You're right, and Tesla agrees so strongly that it built an entire training pipeline around that idea.

I like to think of lidar as a tutor holding a perfect answer key. It measures distance directly by timing laser pulses, so it can grade every guess a camera network makes about how far away something is.

Tesla has designed a system where a special test fleet carries radar and lidar alongside the regular cameras. Every reading is synchronized, so the precise depth and speed from the expensive sensors get attached automatically to the objects the cameras see.

The labeling even uses hindsight. When two cars blur into one blob early in a clip and separate later, the training servers rewind the footage and use the clear moment to label the confusing one correctly.

Tesla applies the same teacher to 3D space itself. Its occupancy network learns from lidar-backed ground truth to predict, for every small cube of space around the car, how far that cube sits from the nearest surface.

That's how plain cameras learn to sketch a sloped curb or a curved bumper smoothly instead of as a pile of blocky Lego bricks.

Even the grading got faster. Tesla designed a cross-labeling trick that draws a box around a car in a flat photo, then projects that box into the laser point cloud as a pyramid of vision, so the software only searches that slice instead of the whole 3D world.

You probably know DeepScale, the startup Tesla acquired in 2019. It was already working out in 2016 how to train cheap sensors to mimic premium lidar data, and Tesla is still pursuing that work today.

Here's the step where our views split.

Once the student has learned, the teacher can stay home. The test fleet keeps the expensive hardware, and the cars customers actually buy ship with cameras only.

Tesla has put real money behind this. In early 2024, lidar maker Luminar named Tesla its largest customer for the quarter, and Elon soon replied on X, "We don't need them even for that anymore."

The student is even learning to write its own answer key. To map the shape of the road surface, Tesla has designed a method that can triangulate ground truth points straight from camera images instead of relying on lidar.

Co-training requires lidar in the classroom, not in every car on the road. With respect, GM's plan keeps the teacher riding along forever.

⚡ ON SPEED, CAMERAS ARE QUICKER THAN THEY LOOK

Your sharpest point is about speed. Radar can measure how fast something is moving in a single snapshot, and a camera can't.

Radar's trick is the Doppler effect, the same physics that makes an ambulance siren sound higher as it rushes toward you and lower as it drives away. Radar reads that pitch shift in its own radio echo to measure closing speed instantly.

A camera has to work speed out from motion. It compares where an object sits in one frame with where it sits in the next, much like you judge a thrown ball by watching it fly.

That sounds slower, but the gap is tiny. Tesla's own designs describe cameras running at rates such as 36 frames per second, which puts a fresh frame in front of the network about every 28 milliseconds, quicker than a single blink.

The physics also cuts both ways. Doppler only measures motion toward or away from the sensor, so a car crossing your path sideways at an intersection produces little to no Doppler shift.

To catch that sideways motion, a radar has to track the car across several scans, which is exactly what a camera does with frames. On that kind of motion, the "instantaneous" advantage disappears.

Radar has another well-known weak spot. Owner's manuals for radar-based cruise control have long warned that the system may not brake for a stopped vehicle, partly because a parked car, an overhead sign and a bridge can all look like the same motionless metal.

Now here's what Tesla has built since you left.

Tesla has designed its vision network to output a full 3D velocity vector for every object, covering speed, direction and even height. It learned that skill from the radar on its test fleet, which turns ordinary cameras into something that behaves like a Doppler radar made of pixels.

Tesla's virtual camera invention goes further by measuring speed in two different ways. Cars are tracked relative to the moving Tesla itself, while pedestrians are tracked against the fixed ground, so the system knows a person's true walking path even while the car accelerates or turns.

When things get fast, the network speeds up its memory. A frame selector pulls video snapshots more rapidly as speeds rise and blends them with the car's own acceleration and yaw rate, which is how quickly the car is rotating, to build a smooth picture of motion over time.

There's also a dedicated sentinel for the car directly ahead. A super-narrow model watches only the closest vehicle in the lane through the narrowest forward lens and keeps estimating its distance, speed and acceleration, which is exactly what you need to brake hard and early.

So yes, a camera infers velocity instead of measuring it in one shot. But inference refreshed every few dozen milliseconds, trained on radar's own answers, and able to see sideways motion that Doppler misses is not a camera ignoring physics.

🌫️ ON FOG, I'LL GIVE YOU THAT ONE, BUT HEAR ME OUT

No camera sees through dense fog, and neither does the human eye. Radar does.

But look closely at your own argument. The near-visible wavelength that you said makes lidar a great teacher is the same reason lidar struggles in fog, because the tiny water droplets that scatter visible light also scatter laser light.

So the fog argument is really a radar argument, and radar alone can't finish the job. It can't read lane paint, a traffic light, a speed limit sign or a flagger's hand signal, so even a car loaded with radar still leans on its cameras when the world turns gray.

That's why I think the real question isn't whether a car can see through fog. The real question is whether the car knows when its vision is degraded, and whether it behaves like a careful driver when it is.

This is where Tesla's visibility invention comes in.

Tesla has designed a separate neural network whose only job is grading its own eyesight. It splits every camera feed into a fine grid and scores each cell from clear to blacked out, building a live heat map of where the car can and can't trust what it sees.

Each camera position gets its own specialist. A model judging the left pillar camera was trained on images from that same pillar location across many other cars, because a windshield camera behind wipers and a fender camera facing tire spray get dirty in very different ways.

The system also diagnoses the cause. It can tell a smear of mud from fog, heavy snow or a hardware fault, then reach for the right fix, such as running the wipers or warming the glass.

When a lens is blinded for a moment, the car doesn't forget the road. Tesla anchors what it saw to fixed spots in the physical world, so a pothole hidden by a truck's spray stays pinned on the car's mental map for those few seconds.

And when conditions really are too much, the car responds the way a good human driver would. It slows down to widen its reaction window, can move to a safer lane, and can hand control back with a plain explanation such as "Due to Heavy Snow, Autopilot is Reducing Speed."

Tesla is also sharpening the eyes themselves. Its designs feed raw, unprocessed sensor data straight into the AI chip, the same idea behind the "photon count" images Elon posted in May, when he said this is why FSD can see so well at night or through extreme glare.

Around the lens, Tesla has designed micro-cone glare shields, corrective windshield patches, pulsed laser cleaning and even gas-absorbing plastics that keep a hazy chemical film off the inside of the glass. Each one attacks a different way a camera can lose its view.

Fog will always be fog. Tesla's bet is a car that measures how blind it is, remembers what it saw, and slows down exactly when a wise driver would.

💸 YES, RADAR IS CHEAP, BUT THAT WAS NEVER THE POINT

You're right that a radar unit doesn't cost much. But Elon's case against it was never about the sticker price.

In April 2021, as Tesla prepared to remove radar, Elon explained it this way: "Sensors are a bitstream and cameras have several orders of magnitude more bits/sec than radar (or lidar)." A second sensor, he added, has to meaningfully improve the signal to be worth the complexity of integrating it.

In August 2025 he put it even more bluntly: "Lidar and radar reduce safety due to sensor contention. If lidars/radars disagree with cameras, which one wins?" In the same post, he wrote that Tesla turned off the radars in its cars to increase safety.

Picture two witnesses to the same moment telling different stories. The radar reports a solid object ahead, the cameras see an empty road under a steel overpass, and the car has a fraction of a second to decide who's wrong.

Trust the radar every time and you get phantom braking under bridges. Trust the cameras every time and the radar was only along for the ride.

Then there's the cost that never shows up on a parts list. Every extra sensor needs calibration, its own data pipeline, fusion software and validation for every way the sensors can disagree, and that burden grows with each new sensor type.

Tesla's own history shows how heavy that lift is. The DeepScale design for mimicking lidar needed separate neural branches for each sensor type just to absorb their different quirks, timing and mounting positions before merging them.

I'd argue the biggest hidden cost is data. Tesla's FSD (Supervised) fleet has logged more than 16.7 billion miles, nearly all of it seen through cameras alone, and a radar channel added today would arrive with none of that history to learn from.

Look at what happened at Volvo this summer. In July, the company confirmed it was dropping lidar from the EX90 and ES90 after cutting ties with its supplier Luminar, which went bankrupt, and Norwegian owners are receiving NOK 18,000 per car for lidar features that never arrived.

Elon's reply was short: "I did try to warn them. Humans drive using neural nets and optical sensors. Same is true for robot cars."

Cheap hardware can turn into an expensive argument, and back in 2021 Tesla decided it would rather not have the argument at all.

🛣️ WHILE YOUR SYSTEM WAITS FOR 2028, CAMERA-ONLY TESLAS ARE ALREADY LOGGING THE MILES

Your plan for handing control back deserves real credit. You said the Escalade won't toss the wheel to a surprised driver, and will instead give a countdown of around ten minutes and pull off at an exit if nobody takes over.

That philosophy should sound familiar, because Tesla's visibility invention describes the same graceful exit. The car slows down first, looks for a safer lane, explains the reason on the screen, and only then hands control back.

The real difference is timing. GM's eyes-off system is still a 2028 promise, while Tesla's camera-only cars are collecting evidence right now.

Tesla's latest FSD (Supervised) safety report shows 6,006,200 miles per major collision in North America, compared with a U.S. average of 660,164 miles. That's roughly nine times as far between airbag-level crashes, measured over a rolling twelve months.

Tesla's new Robotaxi safety report goes a step further. Driverless Teslas with no safety monitor inside have covered 3.1 million miles in Texas and Florida this year, including 862,000 miles after dark and 113,000 miles in rain, with zero people injured by a Robotaxi and zero airbag deployments, based on the crash reports Tesla files with NHTSA.

And that Robotaxi fleet runs on the latest Model Y and the Cybercab, neither of which carries radar or lidar. I find that hard to square with the idea that camera-only driving ignores physics.

🔭 WHERE I THINK WE REALLY DISAGREE

You framed this as physics versus faith, but I think both sides accept the same physics. What we really disagree about is where the intelligence should live.

GM puts more of it in the hardware, stacking sensors so each one covers another's weak spot. Tesla puts it in the neural network, using radar and lidar as teachers in the classroom and then trusting a trained brain behind the cameras.

There's a quiet twist hidden in that choice. A multi-sensor car can only learn from fleets that carry the same sensors, while every camera-equipped Tesla on the road feeds the same classroom.

Physics decides what a sensor can see. Data decides what a car understands.

Best regards,

Ming

P.S. If you're ever in Austin, a driverless Tesla might make my case better than I can, and it won't need lidar to find you.
