• Jan 2026: first rides with nobody from Tesla on board
• April 2026: unsupervised in Dallas and Houston
• July 2026: Miami, Orlando and Tampa

The fleet now
• Texas DMV authorisations: 1,080 Tesla robotaxis. 573 Cybercabs, 507 Model Ys
• Waymo is authorised for 1,207 in Texas

Cybercab
• Unveiled Oct 10, 2024 at We, Robot
• Two seats. No steering wheel, no pedals, no mirrors
• First production car Feb 2026 at Giga Texas. Formal production April
• Paid rides began in Austin on Sept 3, 2026
• NHTSA opened an audit of its self-certification the same day

FSD now
• 3 billion miles in Jan 2025. 10 billion by May 2026
• About 15 billion by the end of September, per Tesla's Q3 report
• 1.74M active FSD subscriptions at the end of Q3, up 67%
• Older HW3 cars can't go unsupervised, Musk admitted in April. A "v14 Lite" began rolling out June 29

FSD in Europe
• April 10, 2026: Dutch regulator RDW approved FSD (Supervised) after 18+ months of tests. Driver assistance, not self-driving
• Since then: Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark, Belgium, Slovenia, Czechia, Croatia, Slovakia and Latvia. 10 EU countries
• Germany, France, Spain and Italy have not
• Oct 9: renamed "Tesla Assisted Driving" in Europe after Germany called the name misleading
• An EU-wide vote is reported for December at the earliest, but not confirmed. It needs 15 of 27 countries

The recovery
• Q3 2026 deliveries: 486,532, above estimates of about 461,000, down 2% on a year earlier
• Record close of $489.88 on Dec 16, 2025
• Nov 2025: shareholders approved a pay package for Musk worth up to $1 trillion if he hits his targets
• Jan 2026: Tesla said it would end Model S and Model X to focus on Optimus

Optimus
• First shown in 2021, prototype in 2022
• Critics say demo robots were partly remote-controlled
• Tesla says Fremont lines are being built for up to 1M robots a year

SpaceX ties
• March 2026: Tesla put about $2B into SpaceX
• SpaceX bought $480M of Tesla Megapacks in nine months, per its filing
• October 2026: both boards formed special committees to study a combination. No deal announced

The Roadster returns
• Promised in 2017: 0-60 in 1.9 seconds, production in 2020. Never built
• Oct 15, 2026: shown at SpaceX's McGregor test site with compressed-air thrusters
• Tesla claims 0-60 in 0.81 seconds
• Musk is targeting 2028 for production. No price yet. Reservations are $50,000 or $250,000

A Tesla share bought at the 2010 IPO cost $17. After two splits, that's $1.13.

On Oct 27, 2026, it closed at $407.46. Roughly 360 times the money.

Video: @Tesla, @robotaxi, @teslaeurope, @Tesla_Optimus, @BloombergTV, @artsimage, @davelee and @MissJilianne

posts.name: Aakash Gupta
posts.text:
Tesla just started sending cars with nobody in the driver's seat out at the exact hours you're most likely to get hit by a drunk driver.

After midnight, more than half the deadly crashes in America involve a drunk driver. During the morning commute it's about 1 in 8.

As of this week, Robotaxi runs until 2am. Back in August the cutoff was 10pm. Tesla has been pushing it back an hour at a time since then, 11pm on October 12, midnight on October 17, 1am last week, and now 2am, right when Texas bars stop serving.

Every hour they added is worse than the one before it. NHTSA's 2023 data has 9pm to midnight at 41% of fatal crashes involving a drunk driver, and midnight to 3am at 56%. Those three hours after midnight are an eighth of the day, and they account for about a fifth of all the drunk-driving fatal crashes in the country.

So it makes sense these were the last hours to go.

At 1am the car is working with less light, and it's sharing the road with more impaired drivers than at any other time of day. Earlier this month Elon said the thing they were still working on for nights was seeing animals in the dark. Grey kittens on grey pavement, specifically. A car with no one behind the wheel has to catch that cat at 1am while the guy who just closed out the bar drifts past it in the next lane, and it has to do that every single time.

Tesla's own safety report already had 862,000 miles driven after dark as of October 18, out of 3.1 million autonomous miles. They didn't flip this on cold.

Now think about who's opening a ride app at 1:45am on Sixth Street. Some of those people drove there. Every one of them who rides home instead is one less drunk driver on the road during the worst hour of the day.

The same update shipped trip sharing, so a friend can watch the map until you're home, and Calm Mode, which dims the screen and the cabin lights. Pretty much what you'd want walking out of a bar at closing time.

And the money side is simple. Going from a 16-hour day to 20 hours gives every car in the fleet 25% more time to make money, and Tesla didn't have to build a single new car to get it.

That leaves 2am to 6am. Ashok Elluswamy said on the October 21 earnings call they're aiming for 24/7 by the end of the year.

posts.name: Gail Alfar
posts.text:
I just took my full self-driving car into downtown Austin to look at the fully autonomous Robotaxis. Just going to share a few of my thoughts.

Cesar Chavez is a Robotaxi corridor. Cybercabs and Model Y cabs on every block, almost every one filled with customers… yet I was able to catch a ride that came to me in less than 2 minutes.

Traffic would jam up in one lane, but the Cybercab would smoothly adjust to a lane with less traffic within one instant. When I needed to change my drop-off spot, it did that instantaneously too. It was less than a block away, but the car made a turn immediately and safely to the new destination. No lag.

I could be watching a video the whole time. All I had to do was voice command Superintelligence in the car: “Find a live concert by the Talking Heads.” (Life During Wartime came on in seconds.) 

I could also listen to music as loud as I wanted. Tesla may have adjusted the volume up.

As far as the space, the Cybercab feels super spacious inside. It might look tiny on the outside, but that’s very, very deceiving. The vehicle is so efficient that the cabin is actually humongous.
And I never have to touch anything. I don’t have to touch the screen. I do not have to touch door handles to enter or exit. 
I can do everything from my own phone app. 
This is great for germophobes. 
And lately, with people getting sick, I’m happy for that.

Tesla’s latest Robotaxi job postings offer some interesting clues about where the company could expand its service next.

Tesla currently operates driverless Robotaxi services in six U.S. cities: Austin, Dallas, and Houston in Texas, along with Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. In California, Tesla also operates a service across the San Francisco Bay Area with safety drivers behind the wheel.

So, where could Tesla expand next?

Tesla has officially listed four additional cities as “Coming Soon”:

- Las Vegas, Nevada
- Phoenix, Arizona
- San Antonio, Texas
- Jacksonville, Florida

However, no specific launch dates have been announced.

Beyond these four cities, Tesla’s hiring activity reveals some interesting developments.

In Fort Worth and Corpus Christi, Texas, as well as Tucson, Arizona, Tesla has posted positions related to Robotaxi fleet support and operations.

Meanwhile, Tesla is also recruiting AI Safety Operators for FSD data collection in Chicago, Illinois; Atlanta, Georgia; and Nashville, Tennessee.

These data collection positions are separate from Robotaxi fleet operations roles.

Personally, I find the locations where Tesla is hiring dedicated Robotaxi operations personnel particularly interesting, especially those outside its officially announced expansion markets.

While job postings don't guarantee an upcoming launch, they may offer valuable clues about where Tesla's Robotaxi network could expand next.

Sources: Tesla Robotaxi Safety Report, Tesla Careers

posts.name: Cole Grinde
posts.text:
WHAT $TSLA HAS ACHIEVED OVER THE YEARS.

2012

“Model S deliveries begin mid-2012.” First customer Model S sedans were handed over at the Fremont factory on June 22, 2012—the world’s first premium EV sedan designed and built from the ground up as electric. 

2015

Autopilot hardware was in cars from late 2014; the first real Autopilot software (lane-keeping + traffic-aware cruise) rolled out in October 2015 with version 7.0. 

2016

Model 3 unveil drew hundreds of thousands of reservations in the first days. Tesla publicly targeted a roughly $35k starting price (before incentives) and delivered the first customer cars in 2017. 

2017

Model 3 production started in July; first customer deliveries occurred the same month. The car became the highest-volume EV Tesla had ever built. 

2018

Tesla hit the 5,000 Model 3s-per-week production rate that Musk had repeatedly targeted. Model 3 became the best-selling EV in the U.S. (and later globally among EVs). Navigate on Autopilot launched. 

2019

Gigafactory Shanghai broke ground in January and produced its first customer Model 3s in December under 12 months from groundbreaking to delivery. Tesla also briefly offered a $35,000 Model 3 Standard Range. 

2020

Tesla achieved its first full calendar year of GAAP profitability and joined the S&P 500. It became the world’s most valuable automaker (passing Toyota). Model Y production began; FSD Beta was released to a limited group of early-access drivers in October. 

2022

First production Tesla Semi trucks were delivered to PepsiCo in December (after the 2017 unveil). Giga Berlin and Giga Texas both began customer deliveries of Model Y. Tesla delivered more than 1.3 million vehicles for the year. 

2023

Model Y became the best-selling passenger vehicle of any kind worldwide (1.22 million units), the first EV to top the global ranking. Cybertruck customer deliveries began in November. 

2024–2025

Energy storage deployments hit successive records (46.7 GWh in 2025). Supercharger network surpassed 70,000–80,000 stalls. FSD (Supervised) cumulative miles crossed multiple billions. Shanghai produced its 4-millionth vehicle. 

2026 (year-to-date)

Tesla produced its 10-millionth vehicle globally. Robotaxi service (initially with safety monitors, later expanding driverless in limited areas) launched in Austin and additional cities. Optimus robots began limited internal factory use. Supercharger network exceeded 85,000 stalls.

posts.text:
Austin, TX AV incident log just came out. Here's the Robotaxi and Waymo incidents reported in October 📝

20 reports: Tesla Robotaxi 8, Waymo 12. Zero collisions for either 💥

Tesla's 8 is its highest month yet in Austin, up from 5 in September 📈

About 6 of the 20 were logged by APD during ACL Fest weekends 👀

🟢 = Nuisance, no road risk 🟡 = Traffic or operational issue 🔴 = Put pedestrians, kids, or first responders at risk

🚕 Tesla Robotaxi - 8 reports

🟢 Empty Robotaxi cut through a private HOA alley off E Riverside (350)
 🟡 ACL: tried to go the wrong way around a shuttle barricade, and police redirected it by hand (336)
 🟡 Cybercab stuck off Lund with its door up (337)
 🟡 3 Cybercabs blocked Lamar near Toomey trying to U-turn in heavy traffic (341)
 🟡 Cybercab drove into the West Riverside Dr construction closure (353)
 🟡 Daily 2nd St gridlock from Teslas and Waymos (346)
 🔴 A line of 10-12 gold Robotaxis didn't yield to an AFD truck running lights and siren, then passed its scene too fast (348)
 🔴 ACL: stopped past the stop line into the Barton Springs/S Lamar crosswalk and tried to back up while pedestrians crossed. Officers blocked it front and back (344)

🚙 Waymo - 12 reports

🟢 Drop-offs in a private apartment driveway (343)
 🟢 Diesel generators at a charging site by the Butler Trail (349, 351 - same complaint logged twice)
 🟢 Rider misrouted and dropped on a dark street with no sidewalk (356)
 🟡 A disabled Waymo drove off when an officer lit it up and took about 2 min to stop (347)
 🟡 Waited in a bike lane, then cut in behind a car (342)
 🟡 Confused by ACL crowds at Barton Springs/Bouldin, and an officer moved it (340)
 🟡 Two Waymos made a two-way street impassable (352)
 🟡 Same 2nd St gridlock report (345)
 🔴 ACL: missed officer hand signals and stalled mid-intersection at Lamar/Barton Springs during a pedestrian crossing (339)
 🔴 Went through the Shoal Creek mid-block crosswalk without slowing for a pedestrian (355)
 🔴 Pulled into the opposing lane around stopped cars while an officer held traffic for kids at Hyde Park Lower School (354)

📊 vs the Texas DMV AV registry: Tesla 8 reports / 1,244 vehicles = 0.64%. Waymo 12 / 1,259 = 0.95% - Not a clean comparison (Austin incidents vs. all Texas AV registrations), but still good to compare the most locally verified fleet size data to incidents

No collisions. Both of Tesla's 🔴 involve reading police and first responders. Waymo's lean toward pedestrians and schools ✍️

✏️ City data = unverified complaints with no fault determined. The date is when the city logged the report.
